claim: ATXN3 colocalizes with PNKP in postmortem brain tissue from patients with HD and control subjects.

evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about the domain structure of PNKP.

claim: The PHOS domain of PNKP hydrolyzes 3'-phosphate groups.
source: The PHOS domain hydrolyzes 3'-phosphate groups, while the KIN domain promotes addition of a phosphate group to the 5'-OH at damaged sites for error-free repair (Karimi-Busheri et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature (Karimi-Busheri et al., 1999) and represents established knowledge about PNKP function.

claim: The KIN domain of PNKP promotes addition of a phosphate group to the 5'-OH at damaged sites for error-free repair.

evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to the literature (Karimi-Busheri et al., 1999) and represents established knowledge about PNKP function.

claim: HTT is present in the FLAG-(FL-PNKP)-IC and FLAG-(PHOS + KIN)-IC but not in FLAG-ICs when the individual FHA, PHOS, or KIN domains were immunoprecipitated.

claim: The C-terminal catalytic domain of PNKP (PHOS + KIN) interacts with HTT.

evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing HTT co-immunoprecipitates with the PHOS+KIN domain but not individual domains.

claim: The individual FHA, PHOS, and KIN domains of PNKP are not sufficient for interaction with HTT.
source: This suggests that the C-terminal catalytic domain of PNKP interacts with HTT, but the individual FHA, PHOS, and KIN domains are not sufficient.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing HTT does not co-immunoprecipitate with individual PNKP domains.

claim: Both wtHTT and mHTT interact with the C-terminal catalytic domain of PNKP.

claim: Transgenic mice expressing exon one or a truncated fragment extending beyond the first exon (N171) with NT-mHTT recapitulate HD-like neurological and behavioral abnormalities.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature (Mangiarini et al., 1996; Schilling et al., 1999).

claim: The N-terminal fragment of HTT (NT-wtHTT-Q23 and NT-mHTT-Q97) forms immunocomplexes with PNKP, ATXN3, and HTT.
source: To test whether this fragment interacts with PNKP, we expressed NT-wtHTT-Q23 or NT-mHTT-Q97 (1–586 base pairs) as a GFP-tagged peptide in SH-SY5Y cells (Figure 4A; upper panel), isolated the NEs, and IP'd the GFP-NT-HTT fusion peptide with a GFP antibody. claim: The N-terminal fragment of HTT (NT-wtHTT-Q23 and NT-mHTT-Q148) forms immunocomplexes with ATXN3, PNKP, POLR2A, CBP, and LIG 3 but not APE1.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The N-terminal fragment of HTT interacts with the C-terminal catalytic domain (PHOS + KIN) of PNKP.

WBs revealed FL-PNKP and PNKP-(PHOS + KIN) domains in the Myc immunocomplex (Figure 4C & D; lanes 1 and 6), suggesting that the N-terminal fragment of HTT interacts with the C-terminal catalytic domain of PNKP.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C & D.

claim: The PNKP-(FHA + PHOS) domain shows a relatively weaker interaction with the N-terminal fragment of HTT.
source: The PNKP-(FHA + PHOS) domain also showed a relatively weaker interaction with the N-terminal fragment of HTT (Figure 4C & D; lanes 5) indicating that the FHA-PHOS domain of PNKP alone interacts with the N-terminal fragment of HTT.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C & D.

claim: BiFC assays show that the N-terminal of mHTT interacts with PNKP.
source: Although these data suggest that the N-terminal of mHTT interacts with PNKP, these experiments do not inform the relative strengths of interaction between these peptides.
evidence: This claim is based on the BiFC assay results described in the text and shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The 3'-phosphatase activity of PNKP was 70–80% lower in the nuclear extract of HD iPSC-derived neurons (mHTT-109Qs) compared to control neurons (wtHTT-33Q).

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A to C.

claim: PNKP protein levels did not change in HD iPSC-derived neurons (mHTT-109Qs) compared to control neurons (wtHTT-33Q).
source: HD iPSC-derived neurons (mHTT-109Qs) were compared to control neurons (wtHTT-33Q; HD iPSC HD iPSC Consortium, 2017) and activity was found to be 70–80% lower in the NE of HD neurons, while PNKP protein levels did not change (representative experiment, Figure 5A to C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: There was substantially reduced (70% to 80%) PNKP activity in HD neurons (Q50 and Q53) compared with control neurons (Q18 or Q28).

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: PNKP activity was about 30–40% higher in the nuclear extract of PC12 cells expressing wtHTT (FL-wtHTT-Q23) compared to control cells.
source: We next measured PNKP activity in PC12 cells expressing exogenous full-length wtHTT (FL-wtHTT-Q23) and full-length mHTT (FL-mHTT-Q148) (Igarashi et al., 2003; Tanaka et al., 2006). We found that it was about 30–40% higher in the NE of PC12 cells expressing wtHTT, and about 70% lower in the NE of PC12 cells expressing FL-mHTT-Q148 compared to control cells, while PNKP protein levels did not change (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A to C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A to C.

claim: PNKP activity was about 70% lower in the nuclear extract of PC12 cells expressing FL-mHTT-Q148 compared to control cells.

We found that it was about 30–40% higher in the NE of PC12 cells expressing wtHTT, and about 70% lower in the NE of PC12 cells expressing FL-mHTT-Q148 compared to control cells, while PNKP protein levels did not change (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A to C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2A to C.

claim: wtHTT stimulates PNKP activity.
source: These data suggest that wtHTT and mHTT stimulate and abrogate PNKP activity, respectively.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing increased PNKP activity in cells expressing wtHTT.

claim: mHTT abrogates PNKP activity.
source: These data suggest that wtHTT and mHTT stimulate and abrogate PNKP activity, respectively.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing decreased PNKP activity in cells expressing mHTT.

claim: In HTT-depleted cells, PNKP activity was reduced by >70%.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2D to G.

claim: wtHTT plays key roles in stimulating PNKP activity, maintaining the functional integrity of the TCR complex, and repairing DNA damage.
source: We found that in HTT-depleted cells, PNKP activity was reduced by >70% (Figure 5—figure supplement 2D to G), suggesting that wtHTT plays key roles in stimulating PNKP activity, maintaining the functional integrity of the TCR complex, and repairing DNA damage.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data showing reduced PNKP activity in HTT-depleted cells.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D to F.

claim: PNKP activity was >80% lower in PC12 cells expressing NT-mHTT-Q148.

claim: PNKP activity was decreased in SH-SY5Y cells expressing NT-mHTT with variable glutamine expansions.

claim: PNKP activity was >80% decreased in the STR and CTX of N171-82Q brain compared to control.

claim: Nuclear extracts from cells expressing mHTT or from zQ175 mouse brain abrogated repair of the DNA duplex that requires PNKP.

claim: In response to DNA strand break accumulations, ATM is activated by phosphorylation which phosphorylates p53, which in turn activates pro-apoptotic gene transcription.
source: In response to DNA strand break accumulations, ATM is activated by phosphorylation which phosphorylates p53, which in turn activates pro-apoptotic gene transcription (Chipuk et al., 2004; Nakano and Vousden, 2001; Oda et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature (Chipuk et al., 2004; Nakano and Vousden, 2001; Oda et al., 2000) and represents established knowledge about the DNA damage response pathway.

claim: There is chronic activation of the DDR-ATM-p53 pathway in HD neurons.

claim: There is chronic activation of the DDR-ATM-p53 pathway in zQ175 CTX.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4C & D.

claim: Deleting p53 in the HD transgenic brain rescues behavioral abnormalities.
source: mHTT expression has been shown to activate p53 in HD, whereas deleting p53 in the HD transgenic brain rescues behavioral abnormalities (Bae et al., 2005).

claim: SH-SY5Y cells expressing NT-mHTT-Q97 showed more DNA strand breaks compared to cells expressing NT-wtHTT-Q23.

claim: DNA strand breaks in cells expressing NT-mHTT-Q97 were substantially rescued after PNKP overexpression.
source: Analysis of mutant cells showed more strand breaks, which were substantially rescued after PNKP overexpression (Figure 5—figure supplement 5A to C), suggesting that mHTT-mediated ablation of PNKP activity contributes to increased DNA strand breaks.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5A to C.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5F.

claim: PC12 cells expressing FL-mHTT-Q148 showed increased caspase-3 activity.

claim: PNKP overexpression reduced caspase-3 activation in PC12 cells expressing FL-mHTT-Q148.

claim: PNKP overexpression significantly rescued cell toxicity in PC12 cells expressing FL-mHTT-Q148.

evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 5H & I.

evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the literature (Chakraborty et al., 2015; Chakraborty et al., 2016; Hanawalt and Spivak, 2008).
